claims.text: Degradation and eventual catastrophic failure are governed by formation and evolution of a non-protective oxide layer.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between the oxide and alloy causes cyclic oxide spallation.
Oxidizing exposure produces a brittle, continuous oxide containing primarily chromium-derived and limited aluminum-derived phases.
The oxide formed under oxidizing conditions delaminates during thermal cycling.
Under reducing atmospheres, absence or transformation of the surface film causes internal oxidation and embrittlement.
The as-built alloy has a uniform fcc matrix.
The as-built alloy may exhibit additive-manufacturing-related microsegregation.
Limited aluminum availability prevents formation of an optimally protective alumina scale and favors chromium-rich oxides.
Oxide spallation or internal oxidation compromises interfacial bonding and creates stress concentrations.
The resulting stress concentrations promote crack nucleation and propagation leading to catastrophic failure.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a relatively continuous but brittle scale that delaminates during thermal cycling.
Reducing exposure will produce less surface oxidation but more internal oxidation and microcracking than oxidizing exposure.
Both oxidizing and reducing exposures will increase crack density relative to the moderate-temperature neutral-gas baseline.
Failure occurs when oxide spallation or corrosion-induced embrittlement sufficiently compromises mechanical integrity.
The proposed mechanism applies above approximately 800 °C, with oxidizing conditions defined as greater than 5% oxygen and reducing conditions as less than 5% oxygen.
Moderate-temperature exposure in neutral gas produces minimal oxidation and crack formation.

contradictions.description: The surface oxide is initially characterized as non-protective, but the reducing-atmosphere pathway subsequently refers to its absence or transformation as the loss of a protective film.
